# Architecture

Open Wallpaper Engine for macOS plays Wallpaper Engine (WE) wallpapers: **scene**, **video** and **web**. The `application` type is out of scope. The goal is to run *any* WE wallpaper, including arbitrary Workshop scenes with custom effects, shaders and SceneScripts. So the scene engine implements WE's actual formats and semantics, not per-wallpaper approximations.

This document describes the structure and the rules for what goes where. Planning notes (the reorganisation steps, feature status, the optimisation log and the per-feature plans that comments cite as "… notes") are kept by the maintainers outside the repository.

## Big picture

```
┌──────────────────────── App shell (SwiftUI/AppKit) ────────────────────────┐
│ App/  Library/  Workshop/  Settings/  UI/            (views + view models) │
└───────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                │ WEWallpaper                    │
      ┌─────────▼─────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──▼──────────┐
      │ Scene/  (engine)  │  │ Video/      │  │ Web/        │
      │  Format  → Values │  │ AVPlayer +  │  │ WKWebView + │
      │  Shaders → Render │  │ music sync  │  │ WE web API  │
      │  Scripting, Audio │  └──────┬──────┘  └─────────────┘
      └─────────┬─────────┘         │
                └──────────┬────────┘
                    ┌──────▼──────┐
                    │ Audio/      │  system capture (process tap or SCK), item taps
                    └─────────────┘
Core/  logging, diagnostics, settings store, asset locations: usable by everything above
```

**Dependency direction:** arrows only point down. Code in `Scene/` must never import or reference anything in `UI/`, `Library/`, `Settings/` views or `AppDelegate`. Code in `Core/` depends on nothing else in the app.

## Targets

- **`OpenWallpaperEngine.framework`** (target OpenWallpaperEngineFramework, module `OpenWallpaperEngine`): all of the app's code, the folders below, with the packages it uses (ShaderToolchain, Sparkle, OWEEditor, OWEControlProtocol, OWETheming, WEFormat). It is embedded once, in the app's `Contents/Frameworks`. The code's own resources are in the framework's bundle and read through `AppBundleLayout.framework`: the Metal library (`SceneMetalLibrary`), SceneScript's JavaScript, the now-playing adapter, the placeholder media and the legal documents. Objective-C goes through the framework's umbrella header (`OpenWallpaperEngine.h`), not a bridging header.
- **Open Wallpaper Engine.app** (target OpenWallpaperEngine) and **Wallpaper Editor.app** (target WallpaperEditor, embedded in `Contents/Helpers`): small executables, the same `OpenWallpaperEngineApp/main.swift`, which calls `AppMain.run()`; the bundle id says which app it is. Each app's bundle (`Bundle.main`) keeps what belongs to the app: its Info.plist, icon, asset catalog and `Localizable.xcstrings`, which SwiftUI, AppKit and `String(localized:)` look up there. The editor finds the framework through its rpath, `@executable_path/../../../../Frameworks`.
- **owe-mcp** (target OWEMCPServer, embedded in `Contents/Helpers`): the MCP Server plugin's command-line server, linking only `Packages/OWEControl` and system libraries (see [`MCP/`](#mcp-packagesowecontrol-and-mcpserver-control-by-mcp-clients)).
- **Open Wallpaper Engine.saver** (target OpenWallpaperEngineSaver, in `Contents/Resources`), the screen saver copied to `~/Library/Screen Savers`. **OpenWallpaperEngineSaverExtension.appex** (a `com.apple.screensaver` app extension, in `Contents/PlugIns`) and **owe-saver-broker** (target OWESaverBroker, in `Contents/Helpers`, with its launch agent in `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents` for `SMAppService`) are the live screen saver's extension transport and its launcher; only release builds embed them (`OWE_EMBED_SCREEN_SAVER_EXTENSION`, see "Lock screen and screen saver"). The savers and the broker share `OpenWallpaperEngineSaver/`'s Foundation-only files (manifests, stamps, XPC messages) with the framework, which compiles them too so the tests reach them.
- **Tests** (`OpenWallpaperEngineTests`) link the framework (`@testable import OpenWallpaperEngine`) and run hosted in the app.

## Modules

These are folders in the framework target today. The scene engine (`Scene/`, `Audio/`, `Core/`) is meant to become a local Swift package (`Packages/WEScene`) during Phase 2, so it can be unit-tested and run headless. Keeping the dependency rules now is what makes that extraction a move rather than a rewrite.

### `Core/`: shared infrastructure

- **Logging and diagnostics:** `OWELog`, signposts and frame metrics.
- **Settings:** the global settings model and store.
- **Wallpaper model** (`Core/Wallpaper`): `WEWallpaper`, `WEProject`, `WallpaperPlacement`, `WallpaperInstanceKey`, `WallpaperPropertyScope`, `WallpaperSettingsIdentity`, `DisplayCanvas` and the storage folder (`WallpaperStorage`). A wallpaper folder's project.json is found and read only through `WEProject.url(in:)` / `read(in:)` (`WEProject+File.swift`; `data`, `object` and `json` for callers that need the bytes or fields `WEProject` doesn't model), which forward to WEFormat's `WEProjectFile`.
- The **WE assets location**.
- **The app's process:** its host context and relaunch (`AppHostContext`, `AppRelauncher`), the helper runs of the app itself (`Core/HelperRun`: `HelperRunCommand`, and `HelperProcess`, which starts one in this process's isolated state), the shared wallpaper services (`Core/Services`, `WallpaperServices`: audio capture and user properties), folder watching (`Core/Files`, `DirectoryChangeWatcher`) and the video memory watch (`Core/Playback/VideoMemoryWatch`).
- The **Objective-C exception catcher**.
- **Element-wise decoding** (`Core/Files/TolerantDecoding`): `decodeElements`, `decodeEntries` and `decodeLogged` skip a bad entry and log it once through `OWELog` (and into a `DecodeFailureLog`, which is WEFormat's). Tolerant JSON and digests as text are in [`Packages/WEFormat`](#packagesweformat-wallpaper-engines-file-formats).
- **Caches** (`Core/Caches`): last use of a cache entry (`CacheEntryUse`, its modification date), what is in use now (`CacheLeases`), the sweeper that expires entries unused for 60 days and clears them (`CacheSweeper`), and macOS's Metal shader cache of the app (`MetalShaderCache`, reset at launch; `DarwinUserDirectories` gives an isolated copy its own). The app's list of caches and their schedule are in `App/Caches` (`CacheFolder+OWE`, `CacheMaintenance`, `MetalShaderCacheLaunch`).
- It must not reference UI, view models or `AppDelegate`.

### `Packages/WEFormat`: Wallpaper Engine's file formats

- The one home for code that reads and writes WE's files, linked by the framework and by the editor package's `OWESceneEditing` (and `OWEEditor`). It depends on nothing in the app and is Foundation only: no `OWELog`, no thread guards, no AppKit images; it returns errors and leaves logging to its callers. Its tests run with `swift test`.
- The framework re-exports it (`Core/WEFormatExport.swift`, `@_exported import WEFormat`), so the framework's files and tests use its types as their own; the editor's files `import WEFormat`.
- **Tolerant JSON** (`TolerantJSON`): `decodeTolerant` (JSON5, so WE's comments and trailing commas), the one UTF-8 byte order mark skip (`TolerantJSON.withoutBOM`, `hasBOM`), and `TolerantJSON.object(from:)`, WE's own reader's tolerance (the mark, comments and trailing commas) for `JSONSerialization` values, which the editor reads its files with. `DecodeFailureLog` collects what element-wise decoding skipped.
- **Digests as text** (`Digest.hex`): the lower-case hex every cache key, cache file name and stamp is spelled in, in the app and the editor.
- **JSON as WE writes it** (`JSON/`): `WEJSONDocument`, JsonCpp's document (integers and reals apart, comments and the byte order mark allowed), and the one JsonCpp styled writer, `WEJSONWriter`, in the two styles WE writes: `generated` (its mobile export: `%.8g` reals, `\uxxxx` for non-ASCII, Windows line ends) and `editor` (the effect and material files its editor writes: shortest reals, characters as they are, `\n`).
- **project.json** (`Project/WEProjectFile`): where a wallpaper folder's project file is and its bytes, its `JSONSerialization` value or root object; the app's `WEProject` helpers and the editor both go through it.
- **Textures** (`TEX/`): `TEXHeader`, the one reader and writer of a `.tex` header (`TEXV0005`, `TEXI0001` with a volume's depth word, `TEXB0001`…`TEXB0004` with the FreeImage format and variant count), `TEXReader` (the words, strings and mipmap records after it) and `TEXContainerWriter` (a header, then mipmap records and whatever a writer adds between them, texture variants' patches). On them: `TEXFileHeader` (a 2D texture's first image's mipmaps), `TEXWriter` (a single-image texture), `TEXFlags`, `TEXImageFormat` and `LZ4BlockEncoder`. Decoding stays in the framework: `TEXParser` (OWELog, thread guards, NSImage), `TEXVolume`, `TEXVariants` and its resolver and writer walk the bytes through `TEXReader` and write through `TEXContainerWriter`.
- **Models** (`Model/`, [`models-plan.md`](models-plan.md) §1): the `.mdl` types (`MDLModel`, `MDLMesh`, `MDLSkeleton`, `MDLAnimation` and the rest) and the one reader, `MDLReader` over `MDLByteReader`, which the player loads models and puppets with and the editor opens a puppet with (`PuppetMDLReader` maps its model onto a `PuppetDocument`; `readWithMeshRanges` gives the byte range of each mesh it keeps byte for byte). Strict, as WE's runtime is. What needs the app stays in the framework: `MDLModel+Load` (the wallpaper's package) and `MDLBonePhysics` (a bone's properties as `SceneJSON`).

### `Scene/`: the WE scene engine

| Area | Responsibility | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `Scene/Format/` | Decode WE files into plain Swift models. It does no rendering and has no side effects. | `scene.json`, `project.json` scene properties, `effect.json`, materials, models, particles, `.pkg`, `.tex` |
| `Scene/Values/` | Resolve every dynamic value the same way: literal, `{"user":…}`, `{"user":{"name","condition"}}`, `{"script":…}`, `{"animation":…}`. User bindings live in one table per loaded scene (`Values/Bindings`). | `UserPropertyBindingTable`, `SceneValueSource` |
| `Scene/Shaders/` | GLSL → SPIR-V → MSL translation (in a helper process, `--shader-compile-helper`), reflection and the translation cache. `FrontEnd/` is the HLSL front end, the one place WE's GLSL-with-HLSL-isms become GLSL glslang takes (see [Shader translation](#shader-translation)). The editors' effect catalog is `EffectCatalog` in `Packages/OWEEditor` (`OWESceneEditing`). | `ShaderVariantTranslator`, `HelperShaderCompiler`, `ShaderCompileHelperServer`, `InProcessShaderCompiler` |
| `Scene/Rendering/` | Metal: layers, the effect pass graph, render targets, text, particles and the camera. | `SceneMetalRenderer`, `SceneShaders.metal` |
| `Scene/Scripting/` | The SceneScript runtime (JavaScriptCore), one per wallpaper instance on its own thread, and the WE JS API surface as extensions; `Host/` ties a runtime to the renderer (docs/scenescript-plan.md). | `SceneScriptRuntime`, `SceneScriptWallpaper`, `SceneScriptSceneMirror` |
| `Scene/Sound/` | Scene sound layers as wallpaper64.exe plays them: each `sound` object's files, its modes and random times, spatialization in the camera's frame, and one `AVAudioEngine` mixer per wallpaper instance, made on first play. | `SceneSoundLayers`, `SceneSoundPlayback`, `SceneSoundMixer`, `SceneSoundSpatialization` |
| `Scene/Prewarm/` | Shader prewarm: a new build compiles the shader variants and effect pipelines of the scenes the user shows into the caches, through the real loader and renderer offscreen, before it replaces the running one. It reads the user's settings and never writes them. | `ShaderPrewarm`, `ShaderPrewarmTargets` (run by `HelperRunCommand`) |
| `Scene/Loading/` | Turns a wallpaper into render content: loads, resolves and builds. `SceneContentLoader` holds the loaded state; its extensions follow the build: `+Loading` (read the scene, `metalContent`), `+LayerBuilders` (image, puppet, solid, text and shape layers; objects scripts create), `+EffectPlans` (materials and effects through WE's shaders), `+Models`, `+Particles`, `+Assets` (JSON, textures, shared assets), `+VideoAsScene`, `+ObjectRebuild` (some objects rebuilt alone) and `+ParticleDocuments` (the Wallpaper Editor's particle documents). | `SceneContentLoader`, `ScenePreparation`, `ParticleSystemBuilder` |
| `Scene/UI/` | Scene-specific SwiftUI: Scene Edit / Export and user properties, and the isolated sessions its export modes edit. These are the **only** scene files allowed to import SwiftUI views. | `SceneInspectorView`, `SceneUserPropertiesView`, `SceneHelp`, `IsolatedSceneEditSession` |
| `Scene/Plans/` | What the loader plans and the renderer draws from: a material's or effect's passes through the translator, a model's meshes. | `ImageMaterialPlan`, `ModelMaterialPlan`, `ParticleMaterialPlan`, `SceneEffectPlan`, `SceneModelPlan` |
| `Scene/Textures/` | "Optimise textures": colour textures prepared as BC7 and cached on disk. | `TexturePreparation`, `TextureCompressor` |

### `Audio/`

- System audio capture (a Core Audio process tap on macOS 14.2+, ScreenCaptureKit before or as the fallback) with a restart lifecycle.
- WE's "Audio recording device": a recording device chosen in Settings › Optimizations › Audio (a microphone, or a loopback driver such as BlackHole) is read by an IO block on that device (`InputDeviceAudioCapture`, Microphone permission) instead of the system output, which stays the fallback while the device is disconnected or the permission is missing. WE's "Recording volume" (0…200, default 50) and "Recording threshold" are applied in the spectrum analyzer, so scenes, SceneScript and web listeners all follow them live.
- Per-player taps (`AudioLevelTap`).
- Wallpaper sound output (`OutputOnlyAudioDevice`): scene sound layers and video wallpapers play on the default output device without its inputs. That is a private stacked aggregate whose one sub-device is the default output device, and it follows that device when it changes. A client of a device that also records (a headset) makes coreaudiod check the Microphone permission, which the app declares for the recording device, and the HAL call waits until the prompt is answered. The stack has no input stream, so playing never asks. The scene engine renders in realtime manual rendering mode and never makes its own `AUHAL`. Instead an IO proc on the stack pulls its frames (`ManualRenderingOutput`), started and stopped on a queue of its own, never on the render thread. The IO proc allocates nothing: its buffers and, when the device runs at another rate, its `AudioConverter` (set up with `AVAudioConverter`'s defaults) are made before it starts. `WallpaperAVPlayer` sets `audioOutputDeviceUniqueID` to the stack, for every player the app makes (`WallpaperAVPlayer.route` for the looping `AVQueuePlayer`s, muted ones too). Unit tests use the stack as well, since a test host is the app and a player there on a headset asked for the microphone with every freshly signed build; only scene sound layers stay off the hardware in tests (`WallpaperServices.sceneSoundOutput` is nil).
- Spectrum and waveform snapshots.
- One producer, many consumers: scene shaders, SceneScript `registerAudioBuffers`, video music sync.
- Now Playing (WE's media integration) is `Scene/Scripting/Media/MacMediaSessionSource`, one per process for scenes, SceneScript's media events and web wallpapers' media listeners. It applies WE's media blocklist: a session of a blocked app (by bundle id, `sessionBundleIdentifier`) reaches them as nothing playing.

### `Video/` and `Web/`

- Each holds its player, view, view model and type-specific features: video music sync, and the web wallpaper property/audio bridge.
- A video wallpaper's player items come from `Video/VideoFileSource`, which follows WE's "Video loading": from disk, or the file read into memory once and served to AVFoundation by a resource loader (`MemoryVideoLoader`, custom URL scheme), so loops read nothing more from the disk.
- **`Web/Chromium/`:** the optional Chromium engine (CEF), installed on demand and pinned by SHA-256. CEF runs only in the `owe-chromium-helper` XPC service (target `OWEChromiumHelper/`), never in the app, and its frames reach the app as IOSurfaces. See [`docs/chromium-engine.md`](chromium-engine.md).
- **Web engine routing:** WebKit by default; Chromium only for a wallpaper that needs it (a Chromium-only API found) while the engine is installed, or when the wallpaper's override says so (`WebEngineRouting`). `WebWallpaperViewModel` drives either engine through `WebWallpaperPage` (a `WKWebView` or a `ChromiumBrowserPage`), so the WE bridge is one implementation. Without Chromium, `ChromiumFeatureAdvisor` points out wallpapers that use Chromium-only APIs (static scan plus WebKit's runtime probe).

### `Library/`, `Workshop/`, `Settings/`, `UI/`, `App/`

- **`Library/`:** app-shell features. It holds the wallpaper library and the import paths (`WallpaperDirectory`, zip/pkg import); the wallpaper model itself is in `Core/Wallpaper`.
  - Installed lists what WE lists (`InstalledLibrary`): items whose project.json `type` is scene, video, web or application. Asset items (`"category": "Asset"`, no `type`) and items downloaded only as another wallpaper's dependency (`WorkshopDependencyIndex`, a hidden file in the library folder) stay on disk, where `WorkshopAssetResolver` finds them, but aren't listed. Downloading such an item yourself makes it yours and lists it.
  - Library folders (Settings › Assets › Library Folders, `LibraryFolders`) are more folders of wallpaper folders the Installed tab lists after the storage folder's: only folders with a project.json, and a Workshop item already listed from an earlier folder isn't listed again. They are read only: nothing is downloaded or moved into them. `LibraryFolderWatcher` lists their changes as they happen.
  - A library entry may be a symbolic link to a wallpaper folder elsewhere, and a library folder may be a link too. A linked wallpaper runs from the folder the link points to (`WEWallpaper`, `ContainedPath.followingFolderLink`), because Foundation's URL listings (`contentsOfDirectory(at:)`, `enumerator(at:)`) don't follow a link they start from. A linked Workshop dependency is resolved the same way (`WorkshopAssetResolver.itemDirectory`). Deleting a linked wallpaper removes the link, never the folder it points to (`WallpaperDeletion`).
  - Installed folders (WE's folders in its Installed tab, not the Library folders above) are `Core/Settings/InstalledFolders`: the tree (`InstalledFolderTree`, WE's operations and the merge every import uses) and its store in `UserDefaults.app`, keyed by `FavoritesStore.key(for:)`. `Library/Folders` scopes the list to the folder shown (`InstalledFolderScope`) and reads WE's own from its `config.json` (`WallpaperEngineFolders`).
  - Deleting a wallpaper removes the dependency-only items nothing left in the library references (`WorkshopDependencyCleanup`, logged). WE leaves required items to Steam, where the user can still see and unsubscribe them; here they are hidden, so keeping them would leave them on disk with no way to remove them.
- **`Workshop/`:** steamcmd and the Workshop API. Steam secrets live in the keychain (`Core/Keychain`, `SteamCredentials`): the Web API key and the steamcmd account name. The password and Steam Guard code are piped to steamcmd on stdin and never stored; steamcmd keeps its own login token. The API key goes in the `x-webapi-key` header, never a URL. An isolated copy (the test host, `OWE_ISOLATED_STATE`) keeps these items in memory (`InMemoryKeychain`) and never calls the keychain, so it can't block on a keychain prompt.
  - Every download lands in the Wallpaper Storage folder as `<storage>/<id>` (`WorkshopItemInstaller`): steamcmd's `force_install_dir` is a hidden `.owe-steamcmd` folder inside it, the finished item is renamed into place and the staging folder deleted. A preview the user applies moves from the preview cache into storage the same way (copied into a hidden folder there, then renamed). A storage folder on a disconnected volume fails the download with that reason; nothing falls back to another folder. steamcmd runs through `SteamCmdRunning`, so tests use a fake.
  - Discover (`WorkshopDiscover`) is WE's static explore lists (`getStaticExploreQueries` in its UI) as the same keyed QueryFiles requests: WE's trend sorts are RankedByTrend with its `days`, and the `Wallpaper` and `Everyone` tags WE adds to every list are sent as exclusions of their siblings, since QueryFiles can't AND required tags. Each list pages on as it scrolls (`WorkshopDiscoverViewModel`).
  - Blocking (`WorkshopBlockList`) is local: blocked items and authors are left out of the Workshop and Discover results. Report opens the item's page in the Steam client or the browser (`WorkshopPageLink`), where the user reports it; nothing is ever posted to Steam for them. "Related Wallpapers" lists the author's items or the presets that require a wallpaper (QueryFiles `child_publishedfileid`).
- **`Installs/`:** what the optional on-demand installs share (the Chromium engine, `Web/Chromium/ChromiumEngineInstaller`, and the depth model, `DepthMaps/DepthMapPluginInstaller`). `VersionedInstallStore` downloads each pinned file, checks its SHA-256, stages the install and renames it into place, keeping the active and the previous version (`VersionedInstallState`); `VersionedInstaller` is the main-actor side (phase, progress, cancel, remove) and `VersionedInstallFailure` the messages for being offline, an HTTP error and a full disk. Each installer keeps only its URLs and files, its install folder and its own step (unpacking the engine, compiling the model).
- **`Settings/`:** settings pages.
- **`UI/`:** the main window and shared components.
- **`App/`:** the entry point, `AppDelegate`, windows and menus.
  - **Identity migration** (`App/IdentityMigration/`): the app's bundle id is `app.openwallpaperengine` (the reverse DNS of openwallpaperengine.app). The first launch under it, before anything reads the defaults (`AppMain`), moves the previous id's state once (`AppIdentityMigration`): the defaults domains (the app's, the editor's), `<Caches>/<id>`, the web views' data, the Steam keychain items (written, read back, then deleted from the old service), the installed screen saver and launch at login. Each step is idempotent and recorded in `<support>/IdentityMigration.json` as it finishes, so a crash resumes. An isolated copy moves only its own tag's defaults, caches and keychain items. `AppIdentityNotice` then says once that macOS asks again for privacy permissions, which can't be moved. See [`docs/releasing.md`](releasing.md#updating-installed-copies).
  - **Command line** (`App/Launch/CommandLineControl*`, docs/command-line.md): WE's `-control` commands. The executable started with `--control <command>` (or WE's `-control`) parses it (`CommandLineControlRequest`), hands it to the running app as a distributed notification named for its isolation (`CommandLineControlChannel`) before any Metal or app lifecycle starts (`AppMain`), waits for the answer and exits. In the app, `CommandLineControlListener` runs it through the MCP Server's `AppControlModel` and the app's own models (`CommandLineControlPerformer`). Play in Window (`App/PlayInWindow`) keeps its windows by name for it.
- Each view model lives next to its view.

### `Editor/` and `Packages/OWEEditor`: the Wallpaper Editor

- The editor is a local Swift package with four modules: `OWESceneEditing` (no UI, and no AppKit or SwiftUI: Foundation, with CoreGraphics, ImageIO and Accelerate for its image work, Combine for the session's, timeline's and authoring models' published state, JavaScriptCore for property conditions, CryptoKit, UniformTypeIdentifiers and simd; the edit overlay over scene.json, the layer outline, gizmo and canvas math, `SceneEditSession` with undo, the draft store `SceneEditDraftStore`, Save as New Wallpaper), `OWEInspectorKit` (controls Scene Edit / Export shares with it) `OWEEditor` (the window's views and their own string catalogs) and `OWEModelImport` (FBX and OBJ import, below). The package depends on nothing in the app but `Packages/WEFormat`, the file formats both link; its tests run with `swift test`.
- `Editor/` is the app's side: the window (`WallpaperEditorController`), whose canvas is the wallpaper's own instance in a preview `WallpaperViewModel`, and the services the module asks for (the user properties view, WE's blend modes, effect help, saving a copy).
- The editor is an **app of its own** inside the app, `Contents/Helpers/Wallpaper Editor.app` (bundle id `<app id>.editor`, target WallpaperEditor, a small executable running the app's framework, `Core/AppBundleLayout`), launched with `--wallpaper-editor <folder>` (`App/Launch/AppLaunchMode`, `AppLaunchPlan`); its delegate (`Editor/Process/WallpaperEditorAppDelegate`) starts none of the main app's launch services and never makes `AppDelegate.shared`. The app launches it through LaunchServices, or asks the running one to open a wallpaper, over the session's distributed notifications (`AppProcessChannel`: a name and a folder, at most with an undo step's name or a timeline command; never the edits). What the editor saves reaches the app's instances through `Editor/Sync/WallpaperEditorChangeSync` (messages plus a watcher on the overlay folder), which posts the same in-process notifications as before.
- **The window edits a draft** (`Editor/Draft/WallpaperEditorDraft`), never the wallpaper: the overlay as edited (`<supportDirectory>/editor/Drafts/<identity>.json`, `SceneEditDraftStore`, there only while it differs from the saved overlay) and the Details panel's user properties (the isolated store `WallpaperPropertyScope.editorDraft`), both written as they change, so a crash keeps them and the next opening offers Resume or Discard. The canvas alone runs it: its preview runs that property scope (`WallpaperViewModel.previewPropertyScope`), whose scenes read the draft (`SceneContentLoader`), and the draft's notifications carry `draft: true`, which only such instances take (`SceneWallpaperInstance.runsEditorDraft`); the displays, the screen saver and playlists run the saved overlay. File › Save (`WallpaperEditorController.saveDraft`) commits both halves and the running instances reload once; Save as New Wallpaper bakes the draft into a new library wallpaper; Revert to Saved goes back to the last save as one undo step. Closing or quitting with unsaved changes asks Save / Don't Save / Cancel, and the close button shows the edited dot. Imported files stay in `<identity>.assets`: they are named by their content, so nothing running sees one until a saved overlay names it.
- Edits are an overlay per wallpaper (`<supportDirectory>/editor/<identity>.json`, `Scene/Loading/SceneEditOverlayFiles`), never written into the wallpaper, with the files the editor added beside it (`<identity>.assets`, `EditorAssetStore`), which the scene loader reads after the wallpaper's own (`SceneContentLoader.wallpaperData`). `ScenePreparation` applies the overlay (layers added, deleted and reordered, effects added and reordered, every field and effect value) before Scene Edit / Export's edits, and the scene cache key covers it.
- A change of values the renderer takes per frame (a layer's transform, opacity and colour, an effect's visibility and constants) is drawn live: the instance measures the editor's overlay against the one its scene was read with (`SceneEditLiveValues`, `SceneWallpaperInstance+EditorLive`) and the renderer applies the difference (`SceneEditorLive`: transforms like user bindings, effect constants as writes under the scripts'). Anything else reloads the instance: the canvas for each change of the draft (a gizmo drag drawn as it goes), every running instance of the wallpaper for a save.
- **The View menu** (`OWEEditor/Canvas/EditorViewCommand`, `EditorViewOptions`; the app's `WallpaperEditorMenu.viewMenu` builds it from the package's list and sends `WallpaperEditorCommands.Command.view`) follows Wallpaper Engine's editor View menu and canvas toolbar (`ui/dist/scripts/scripts.js`): Reset Camera (the canvas fitted), Preview Aspect Ratio (4 : 3, 16 : 10, 16 : 9, 21 : 9) for Show Desktop Preview, Show Phone Preview (9 : 16; a preview dims what such a screen wouldn't show and hides the handles, as WE turns its gizmo off), Show Grid, Show Selection Box, Show Debug › Show Particle Collision (`ParticleCollisionShape`, placed as `ParticleCollision.placed` places them) and Show Particle Control Points, and Low FPS Simulation, which caps the canvas's instance at WE's 22 frames a second (wallpaperui.exe 0x140088b6e; `SceneWallpaperInstance.frameRateCap`, through the pacing's cap). The grid, selection box, collision, ratio and low-FPS settings are kept in the editor's preferences (`WallpaperEditorServices.preferences`); the previews last while the window is open. Show Debug › Show Hitboxes draws the puppets' posed hit boxes (`PuppetHitBoxOverlay`, from the canvas renderer's `ScenePuppetHitBoxFeed`, which a frame fills only while the overlay reads it). WE's Show Collision Capsules (models' capsules) waits for those to reach the editor; Show Axis is WE's particle editor's.
- **Selection** (`SceneEditSession+Selection`): `selection` is the layer the inspector shows; `selectedLayers` every selected one (Shift- or ⌘-click on the canvas or in the list, a marquee from an empty place, `layers(in:)`), and setting `selection` alone selects only it. Option-click goes down through stacked layers (`layer(at:below:)`). Dragging, nudging, deleting and duplicating take the selection, less the layers a selected group carries (`selectedRoots`); a drag of several is `groupDragPreview`, committed as one undo step (`setTransforms`, `endGroupDrag`). **Context menu commands** follow Wallpaper Engine's editor UI (`ui/dist/scripts/scripts.js`: `callbackAssetContextMenu`, `contextMenuPropertyEffect`; `SceneEditSession+LayerCommands`): Center and Align with Background (WE's `centerRenderable`: the origin to the scene's centre plus the image model's `cropoffset`, a layer in a group to its parent's origin), Rotate CW and CCW (∓90° about z), Copy and Paste Transforms (origin, scale, angles), Move to Custom Position (a list row, top-level layers only), Copy and Paste all Effects, and per effect Copy, Paste, Paste Effect Settings (same effect file only) and Duplicate (just after it). The copies are the window's (`EditorTools`), as WE keeps them in its editor. WE 2.8's Isolate Effect is commented out of its UI, so there is none.
- **Effect gizmos** (`OWESceneEditing/Effects/EffectGizmo*`, `OWEEditor/Canvas/EffectGizmoCanvas`): the editor reads an effect's `effect.json` `gizmos` (`EffectGizmo`: Wallpaper Engine's EffectPerspectiveUV, EffectSpinUV, EffectSwingUV, EffectPointEmitter and EffectLineEmitter, each with the constants its handles set and the combo values it shows for) and its shaders' `"position": true` and `"direction": true` constants (`SceneEffectParameters`, into `EffectSchema`). While an effect is open in the inspector (`EditorTools.expandedEffects`), the canvas draws its gizmos on the layer in the layer's UV (`EffectGizmoLayout`, as the shaders read it: Spin and Swing aspect-corrected, emitters' angle 0 up and clockwise) and a drag sets the constants as one undo step (`SceneEditSession.setEffectConstants`); a position constant no gizmo sets gets a point of its own. The inspector shows a position as X and Y, a direction as a dial (in degrees where the shader asks, `"conversion": "rad2deg"`).
- **The canvas gizmo** (`OWESceneEditing/Gizmos/`, `OWEEditor/Canvas/`) has Wallpaper Engine's modes, picked in the canvas's upper left corner as WE's editor UI (`ui/dist/scripts/scripts.js`, `setGizmoMode`, `gizmoOrientation`) has them (`GizmoMode`: Multi in 2D scenes, Translate, Rotate, Scale, and none by clicking the active one; `EditorTools.gizmoMode`), each mode with its own World or Local Space (`EditorTools.gizmoSpaces`; only Translate and Rotate can switch, Translate starting in World Space). A 2D scene's is `LayerGizmo` over the layer's rectangle. A 3D scene's (`Gizmo3D`) sits on the object's origin through the camera its renderer drew the last frame with (`SceneMetalRenderer.lastPerspectiveCamera`, under its own lock, handed to the package as `EditorSceneCamera` through `WallpaperEditorServices.sceneCamera`), opening in Translate; the object's world matrix composes its parents' with WE's rotation order (`LayerSpatial`, `EditorMatrix4.local`), and a turn is written back as WE's angles (`EditorMatrix4.angles`). Clicking near an object's origin picks it.
- Scripting and user-property authoring (P6) live in `Scripting/` and `Properties/` subfolders of `OWESceneEditing` (the overlay's `SceneAuthoring`, the SceneScript typings and autocomplete, the syntax check, templates, `UserPropertyDraft` and its conditions, groups (`UserPropertyGroup`) and the texture slots a `scenetexture` or `usershortcut` property links in the layer material's first-pass `usertextures`, as WE's editor writes them, or `instance.usertextures` for a shared material and older drafts) and of `OWEEditor` (the script editor, binding sheet, property editor and preview); the app's `Editor/Scripting/SceneScriptConsoleTap` hands the runtime's console lines and errors to an open editor. The script editor's Snippets and Edit menus are text edits in `SceneScriptSourceEdits`; Replace Script's snippets (`SceneScriptSnippet`) are WE's own from the user's WE copy when it has them (`EditorScriptTools`: `ui/dist/monaco/snippets`, or the assets cache's `snippets`), else the editor's; Stop Preview holds the canvas's scripts (`SceneRendererScripts.isSuspended`) and applies the content again.
- **Adding layers** (`SceneLayerFactory`, the toolbar's `AddLayerMenu`, `LayerActions+Add`): the objects WE's Add Asset dialog makes, as WE's scenes write them: image, text, sound, light (WE's new light by scene kind), model (a `.mdl` of the wallpaper or of WE's assets, `EditorWallpaperResources.modelChoices`), camera (framing the scene's `camera`), solid, Solid Placeholder (an instanced solid model kept in the edits' files), composition, fullscreen and Full Composition (`projectlayer`, 2D only). WE's presets split by what they add (`ParticlePresetCatalog.Contents`): particle-only variants go to Add Particle System, the others (Clock, Countdown, the light-shaft shapes) to Add Layer › Preset, which copies their files and built-in effects into the edits' files and adds their objects in one undo step (`SceneEditSession.addLayers`).
- **Effects made in the editor** (`OWESceneEditing/Shaders/`, `OWEEditor/ShaderEditor/`): Add Effect's New and Duplicate (`CustomEffectActions`) copy WE's blank effect (`effects/_empty`, from the user's assets) or the chosen effect into `effects/<id>/` as WE's editor does (`CustomEffect.make`: the folder name from the author's name, a one-material effect's material and shader renamed after it, JSON as JsonCpp's styled writer writes it, WEFormat's `WEJSONWriter` in its `editor` style, `SceneJSONValue.editorJSON`). The files are text in the overlay (`SceneEditOverlay.effectFiles`), so they are part of the draft, of undo, of File › Save and of Save as New Wallpaper (`editorFiles`); the loader reads them before any other file (`editorFileData`, also the effect's own folder through `readWallpaperFile`), and a change of them is never drawn live (they are part of `structureOnly`): the canvas reads the scene again. Add Effect lists them, and the wallpaper's own `editable` effects, as My Effects (`EditorWallpaperResources.ownEffects`).
- **The shader editor** (`ShaderEditorModel`, `ShaderEditorPanel`, docked under the canvas; `CustomEffectSection` lists an editable effect's shaders in the inspector): `CodeEditorView` with `CodeEditorLanguage.shader` (`ShaderTokenizer`, `ShaderLanguage`'s completions), WE's Snippets menu (`ShaderSnippets`: WE's insertion rules and annotations; Replace Shader reads WE's `ui/dist/monaco/snippets` at runtime, `EditorShaderSnippets`). Apply writes the file into `effectFiles`, so the canvas reloads with it, and asks the app's translator through `ShaderChecking` (`EditorShaderChecker`: `ShaderVariantTranslator.variant` on the shared translator, then on failure the steps one by one to find the failing step's text); each error's line is mapped back to the edited file through the prelude, the loader's inlined includes and the front end's edits (`ShaderLineMap`). Under the shaders, each material's Shader Options (`MaterialShaderOptions`: `blending`, `cullmode`, `depthtest`, `depthwrite` of its passes) are written into the edits' copy of the material the same way.
- **Importing images** (`TextureImportOptions`, `EditorAssetStore+Textures`, the `ImportOptionsSheet`): WE's importer choices (format, Pixel Art, No Mip Maps, Clamp UVs, Crop transparent area, normal map, image sequence). Where they are WE's defaults a PNG or JPEG is kept as it is; otherwise the store asks its `EditorTextureEncoding`, the app's `EditorTEXEncoder` (`TEXWriter`, `BCBlockEncoder` for DXT1/DXT5, `LZ4BlockEncoder`), for a `.tex`: a still texture, an animated GIF's or a sequence's sprite sheet with its `TEXS0003` frame table, an MP4 as a video texture in WE's layout (`TEXFlags.video`, FreeImage format -1, the MP4 as the one mipmap; `MP4TrackSize` gives the layer its size), a normal map as RG 88. `EditorTEXEncoderTests` reads each back with `TEXParser`.
- **Importing models** (`OWEModelImport`, `OWESceneEditing/Models/`, [`model-import.md`](model-import.md)): FBX and OBJ files are read with ufbx (`Vendor/ufbx`, a local package the editor package depends on) into a `ModelSource`, which `ModelCompiler` writes as WE's resource compiler writes a `.mdl` (Assimp's triangulation, normals, tangent space and vertex joining; a skinned model's bones, bone boxes and sampled animations; the configuration's clips, events, attachments and bone physics). `EditorAssetStore+Models` keeps the source, its configuration (`models/<folder>/<name>.json`, WE's keys), the `.mdl` and `generic4` materials with their textures in the edits' files; `WEDefaultProjectModelTests` compares the output with WE's default projects' models. The Model Editor (`OWEEditor/ModelEditor/`, a model layer's Configure Model…) edits that configuration and the model's materials (`ModelShaderSchema` reads a shader's annotations) and compiles the model again under a new name, pointing the layers at it. Add Layer › Model's Import FBX or OBJ… and model files dropped on the canvas import and add one (`LayerActions+Models`).
- **Project tools** (`ProjectCleaner`, `EditorAssetStore+Materials`, `ProjectToolsMenu`, `ExternalImageEditor`): Clean Project lists the edits' files that nothing names, starting from the draft, the saved overlay and the scene and following every used JSON file (a name matches a path, the path without its extension, or either without its first folder, as WE names textures and shaders), and moves the chosen ones to the Trash. Clean Local Storage forgets the wallpaper's SceneScript stores (`SceneScriptStorage.removeStores`) and reloads the canvas. Edit with External Image Editor writes the layer's texture as a PNG under `<caches>/editor/External/<identity>`, opens it in the app kept in `UserDefaults.app`, watches the folder and imports each save as the layer's `image` and `size`.
- The particle editor (`Particles/` in both modules) keeps particle definitions and materials it wrote in the overlay; the view model reads them before any file (`setEditorAssets`), and a change of those documents alone rebuilds only the particle objects that read them (`particleObjectIDs(using:)`, `rebuildObjects`) instead of reloading the scene.
- **Browser previews** (`Previews/` in the app and in both modules): Add Effect's and Add Particle System's tiles show previews the app's renderer draws in a helper (`--render-editor-previews`, `EditorPreviewRenderer`), cached per WE assets build and per kind's revision (`EditorPreviewCache`; the app's version isn't in the key, so updates keep them). A built-in effect is shown on the editor's test card set as WE's own preview of it sets it (`effect.json`'s `preview` project: its first visible instance's values, held to their sliders' ranges, combos and masks). The main app pre-warms every one in the background (`EditorPreviewPrewarm`): at launch when any is missing and whenever the assets change, every effect then every particle system in the browsers' order, on two lanes that each keep one helper fed over its standard input (`--render-editor-previews -`, `EditorPreviewHelperLane`) and in the background state but for a browser's tiles, paused under `PowerPolicy.allowsEditorPreviewPrewarm` (the rule background renders follow). It is resumable (cached previews are skipped) and incremental: a new build or revision carries over each preview whose inputs' fingerprint (`EditorPreviewInputs`, recorded in the folder's `.inputs.json`) didn't change. While it renders it holds `EditorPreviews/.prewarm.lock`; an editor window that finds it held posts its missing tiles (`EditorPreviewWants`), which jump the queue, and renders whatever is left itself once the lock is released.
- **Thumbnails** (`Thumbnail/` in both modules): Take Snapshot and Record GIF (`EditorThumbnail`) ask the app for the canvas's scene drawn again offscreen at a pixel size (`WallpaperEditorController.drawCanvas`, the screenshot path `SceneRenderLoop.captureScreenshot`), at the scene's aspect, and `ThumbnailEncoder` keeps its centre square: a JPEG, or a GIF from `GIFEncoder` (WE's `gifenc` output: one median-cut global palette, optional Floyd–Steinberg, disposal 1, looping; 32 pixels smaller and 128 colours a step while over Steam's 1 MB). WE's formats are `GIFRecordingFormat.all`, from its `wallpaperui.exe` table. `LocalWallpaperWriter.writeThumbnail` writes `preview.jpg`/`preview.gif` and project.json's `preview`: Save as New Wallpaper into the copy, File › Save into a wallpaper of the user's own in the storage folder (`savesThumbnailInPlace`); a Workshop item is never written.
- **Stats** (`Stats/` in the app and `OWEInspectorKit`'s `RenderStats*`): WE's "Stats per frame" over the editor's canvas (Never / Auto / Always) and a compact readout in Scene Edit / Export. A `RenderStatsFeed` is watched by the views that show it; while it is, `SceneRenderStatsSampler` sets the scene renderer's `frameStats` (`SceneFrameStatsRecorder`), whose frame command buffer is wrapped (`SceneStatsCommandBuffer`: stand-ins that count draws, passes, pipelines, textures and copies and forward everything else), and reads the numbers twice a second. Unwatched, `frameStats` is nil and frames use the real command buffer.
- **New Wallpaper** (`NewWallpaper/` in both modules, the app's `App/NewWallpaper/NewWallpaperWizard`): the library's New Wallpaper… sheet (`NewWallpaperSheet`) makes a folder in the Wallpaper Storage folder through `NewWallpaperBuilder`: a scene from a picture (resized to one of WE's Workshop resolution tags, `NewWallpaperResolution`), an empty scene, a copy of one of WE's 2D templates (`WallpaperTemplate`, read from the assets cache's `templates` or an install's `projects/templates`) with its pictures replaced, or a web wallpaper from a folder; a scene then opens in the Wallpaper Editor.
- **Scene Options and Project Settings** (`Inspector/` in both modules): the inspector's rows with nothing selected edit scene.json's `general` through the overlay (`SceneEditSession+General`: `setGeneral`, WE's defaults in `SceneGeneralSetting`, the resolution as `orthogonalprojection`), grouped as WE's `wallpaperui.exe` groups them; the title is a project.json edit (`SceneEditOverlay.project`, `SceneProjectEdits`), which Save as New Wallpaper suggests and File › Save writes into a wallpaper of the user's own (`LocalWallpaperWriter.writeProjectEdits`). The player reads `general` when the scene is read, so a change reloads the canvas.
- **Layer fields** (`Inspector/` in both modules): the image and sound fields WE's inspector shows write scene.json fields through `SceneEditSession.setValue` (`LayerFieldRows`); Lighting & Reflections edits the material the image layer's model names (`ImageLayerLighting`), kept in the overlay's `documents` by path. The scene loader reads them with the particle editor's documents in place of the files (`SceneEditOverlay.editorFileData`, `setEditorAssets`), a change of one reads the scene again (`SceneEditLiveValues`), and Save as New Wallpaper writes them into the copy (`editorFiles`).
- Depth maps (`DepthMaps/` in the app and in both modules, [`docs/depth-maps.md`](depth-maps.md)): one `DepthMapGenerator` per process runs the plugin's Core ML model off the main thread and releases it after five idle minutes; both editors' Depth Map section writes the map and WE's Depth Parallax effect into the wallpaper's editor overlay (Scene Edit / Export through an edit session of its own), so the two share them.
- **Image tools** (`ImageTools/` in both modules, [`docs/image-tools.md`](image-tools.md)): WE's image preparation as its editor runs it on the picture (OpenCV's operations in `ImagePlane`, `DistanceTransform`, `Inpainting`): Normal Map Generation (`NormalMapGenerator`, the inspector's Normal Map section) writes `<texture>_normal` and a copy of the layer's material using it (`SceneEditSession.applyNormalMap`); Foreground Separation (the layer menu's Image Editing, `SeparationEditor`, `ForegroundSeparator` with `GrabCut` and `MaxFlowGraph`, Vision's foreground objects as its starting guess, `ForegroundPrior`) replaces the layer's picture with the background and adds the foreground above it (`SceneEditSession.applyForegroundSeparation`); Character Sheet Creation (`CharacterSheetModel`, `CharacterSheet`) separates limbs in WE's hierarchy, lays the pieces out as `<texture>_sheet` in place of the layer (`SceneEditSession.replaceWithCharacterSheet`) and opens Puppet Warp on it.
- **Texture variants** (`OWESceneEditing/Assets/TextureVariants/`, `OWEEditor/Inspector/TextureVariants/`): an image layer's variants are a `TextureVariantDocument` (groups of options: file, Replace or Alpha blended, a bool or combo condition), kept as the `.tex-json` beside the compiled texture with the base texture it goes over (`source`), as WE keeps `variants` in a `.tex-json`. Each change compiles them (`SceneEditSession.applyTextureVariants`; the encoder's `texture(_:withVariants:)`, the app's `EditorTEXEncoder+Variants`: each option's file made into a texture of the base's layout, then `TEXVariantWriter` writes the `TEXB0004` option records and the per-mipmap patches `TEXVariantResolver` reads: as WE 2.8's compiler writes them, checked against its own file (capture 540, `Tests/Fixtures/TextureVariants/540`): groups and option ids from 1, every option a patch of the whole mipmap in every mipmap, stored as the mipmap is (a PNG in the PNG container a picture base becomes, raw or LZ4 in a raw texture), Replace blend 0, Alpha blended blend 1, a video's option blend 2) into the edits' files, named by content, through a copy of the layer's material and model, one undo step. Preview sets the Details panel's values (`EditorUserPropertyValues`, `EditorUserPropertyUndo.set`); the player's binding table then rebuilds what reads the texture. Only a texture the editor imported takes variants (its PNG or JPEG beside it, or a `.tex` in the edits), as WE's editor. Clean Project follows a used `.tex-json` to the options' files.

### `MCP/`, `Packages/OWEControl` and `MCPServer/`: control by MCP clients

- The **MCP Server** plugin (Settings › Plugins, `MCP/MCPServerPlugin`), off until installed. Installing copies the app's `Contents/Helpers/owe-mcp` (target OWEMCPServer, `MCPServer/main.swift`) into `<supportDirectory>/Plugins/MCP` with an `install.json` naming the app, and opens the control socket; removing closes it and deletes the folder. See [`docs/mcp.md`](mcp.md).
- `Packages/OWEControl` depends on nothing in the app. `OWEControlProtocol` (linked by the framework and by `owe-mcp`) is the control channel: newline-delimited JSON requests and responses with a version, over a Unix domain socket at `<supportDirectory>/Control/control.sock` (folder `0700`, socket `0600`, peers checked with `getpeereid`), which an isolated copy keeps in its own support folder. `OWEMCP` (only `owe-mcp`) is the MCP server: JSON-RPC over stdio, the tools' schemas and argument checks, and starting the app when no socket answers.
- The app's side: `ControlRequestRouter` checks a request's parameters and resolves wallpapers, displays and playlists; `AppControlModel` (behind the `ControlAppModel` protocol, which tests fake) does what the app's own controls do, on the main actor. `owe-mcp` never reads or writes the app's state itself. The other areas are request groups (`ControlRequestGroup`): `MCP/Scene` (the editors), `MCP/Library` (playlists, metadata, displays, settings, plugin status) and `MCP/System` (Live Photo export, the screen saver, the lock-screen picture), each behind a protocol its tests fake.
- **Headless edit sessions.** A client edits a scene through `HeadlessSceneEditService`: one `HeadlessSceneDocument` per wallpaper holds a `SceneEditSession` over the wallpaper's Wallpaper Editor draft with its own undo stack, applies `scene_apply_edits` lists all or nothing as one undo step (on a copy of the session first, through the same session calls as the editors' controls, `SceneEditOperations`), and writes each change into the draft as the Wallpaper Editor's window does. `WallpaperEditorChangeSync` announces it to the editor's process (`app.overlayDidSave`), whose open window of the wallpaper takes it as an undo step (`WallpaperEditorController.adoptSavedOverlay`); a draft changed elsewhere starts the document over with a fresh undo history. `wallpaper_editor_save` commits the draft as File › Save does: the app's instances apply it once and the window hears it (`app.draftDidSave`).

### `Theming/` and `Packages/OWETheming`: macOS in the wallpaper's colour

- Settings › General › Theming ([`docs/theming.md`](theming.md)): the main display's wallpaper's scheme colour (or its picture's main colour) for the menu bar, the accent and highlight colours, the tinted icon style and the folder colour.
- `Packages/OWETheming` depends on nothing in the app (Foundation, Core Graphics, ImageIO): the colour and OKLab, the accent palette, the menu bar strip's geometry and drawing, the preference values, and `SystemThemeApplier`, which saves the user's values before the first change and restores them. Every write goes through `SystemAppearanceWriter`; its tests use a fake, and an isolated copy of the app a writer that never writes.
- `Theming/` is the app's side: `ThemingController` (when to apply, debounced; owned by the app's delegate) and `DesktopPictureTheming`, the one hook in the per-display desktop pictures `DesktopPictureSync` draws (the menu bar strip).

### `Resources/`

- `Assets.xcassets`, the app icon (`AppIcon.icon`), the legal documents (`Legal/`), SceneScript's JavaScript and media. `Localizable.xcstrings` is in `OpenWallpaperEngine/` itself.
- No Wallpaper Engine files ship in the repository or the app. `Core/WallpaperEngineAssets` resolves them at runtime: a WE install the user chose, else the cache in the Wallpaper Storage folder (`<storage>/.owe-assets`, filled by `Workshop/WallpaperEngineAssetsService` from the user's Steam copy through SteamCMD), else none (scenes show that they need them). Tests read them only from `OWE_ASSETS`.

## Scene data flow

1. **Load.** `Scene/Format` decodes `project.json`, `scene.json` (from disk or the `.pkg`, with the Wallpaper Editor's overlay and Scene Edit / Export's edits applied, `ScenePreparation`), then models, materials, effects and textures (`.tex`).
2. **Resolve.** `Scene/Values` binds user properties (per wallpaper), scripts and animations to typed values. Nothing downstream reads raw JSON or string-keyed dictionaries.
   - Every `{"user": …}` of scene.json and of every JSON document the build reads (effects, materials, particle systems, models, Workshop dependencies, WE's assets) is recorded in the scene's `UserPropertyBindingTable`, with its path, the typed target it drives and a class: `uniform` (a shader constant, updated in place), `object` (a transform, colour, visibility, particle override or script-read value: the object's state updates) or `structural` (a combo, texture, size or anything unrecognised: the object is rebuilt alone, `SceneObjectReplacement`). The parsers decode the table's resolution of each document, so none can drop a binding.
   - *Texture variants* (`TEXVariants`) aren't JSON: the resource compiler bakes a `.tex-json`'s `variants` into the `.tex` (`TEXB0004`'s option records, each with a `{"condition": …}`, and patches after every mipmap). The table resolves a `.tex` read like a document (`resolvedData`): `TEXVariantResolver` composes the options the properties turn on into an ordinary texture, and the conditions are recorded as structural bindings of every object that read it. Every other reader (`TEXParser`) sees the base.
   - *Texture user properties* (`SceneUserTexture`): a plain-string `usertextures` entry (an image object's `instance`, else its material's pass) names a `scenetexture` property; the picked file replaces the image slot. The binding is recorded as a structural one of the object (document `usertextures:<id>:<slot>`), so a new pick rebuilds it alone.
   - A property change is looked up in the table (`SceneBindingUpdate`). The owners it touches move to a new binding revision (`SceneBindingRevisions`), which every cache of a bound value keys on. Only the app's own keys, scene-wide structure (`general`) and objects the scene's stages hold (lights, sounds, models, cameras) rebuild the content; editing properties ends with one rebuild, the reconcile.
3. **Build.** `Scene/Loading` produces render content: an ordered layer list in authored object order. Each layer carries its full parent transform, its effect pass graph (from `effect.json` passes, `fbos`, `bind`, `target` and combos; a pass, bind or FBO with `conditions` is kept only when the pass's combos meet them, in WE's `{COMBO: n}` form or its 2.x form `{COMBO: {"op": "ge"|"gt"|"le"|"lt", "value": n}}`) and its text, particle and sound state.
4. **Render.** `Scene/Rendering` executes the pass graph each frame through translated WE shaders. Uniforms come from reflection, plus built-ins such as `g_Time`, resolutions, pointer and audio spectrum, plus resolved constants.
   - *Scene target size* (`SceneRenderResolution`): Settings › Performance › Render Resolution (`GSRenderResolution`) alone chooses what the target is drawn for: **Your Display**, the displays' backing pixels (1920×1080 on a 1× 1080p display, 5120×2880 on a 5K iMac); **4K**, the long side 3840 at the display's shape, fitted to the display by the composite (supersampled on a smaller one); **Full**, the wallpaper's authored size, placed as WE places it. The scene covers that size exactly, larger or smaller than authored (a scene of the display's shape gets exactly its pixels); only the GPU's texture limit (16384) caps it. A target that follows a live-resizing window (Scene Edit / Export and Wallpaper Editor previews, `SceneMetalRenderer.followsLiveResize`) rounds its pixels per unit up to eighths so a resize doesn't reallocate it every frame. **Upscaling** (`GSUpscaling`) then draws Render Scale (75, 67 or 50 %) of each side, and the final composite scales it up bilinearly. Upscaling is off by default and in every quality preset. MetalFX's spatial scaler was removed: measured, it cost more GPU time than drawing natively (Snowy Plains at 5120×2880: 5.17–5.30 ms against 1.62 ms), and a stored MetalFX choice reads as bilinear at the same scale (`GlobalSettings.migrateMetalFX`). Automatic Texture Resolution weighs the size drawn for (`SceneRenderSettings.renderedPixels`). Exports, settings-less renderers and the tests never draw below the authored size (`SceneRenderSettings.floorsAtAuthoredSize`); screenshots draw at their own size.
   - *Effect Detail* (`GSSceneDetail`, `SceneEffectDetail`): Match Display runs each layer's effects at most at the layer's size on screen; Full at its texture's size, as WE. It doesn't size the scene target.
5. **Script.** `Scene/Scripting` runs once per frame in one context per wallpaper instance, on its own thread. Layer objects read and write a shared object table; the renderer feeds it each object's drawn values before the frame and draws what scripts wrote after it (`SceneRendererScripts`).

### Shader translation

Every shader (effects, image and model materials, puppets, particles) takes one path, `ShaderVariantTranslator.variant`: WE compiles its dialect as HLSL (FXC), so the HLSL front end (`Scene/Shaders/FrontEnd`, `HLSLFrontEnd`) applies FXC's rules, then glslang compiles the pair as one program under its relaxed Vulkan rules and SPIRV-Cross writes the MSL and the reflection (`Vendor/ShaderToolchain`).

1. Includes, `#require`s and combos (`ShaderSourceLoader`, `ShaderVariantTranslator.resolveCombos`); the prelude maps HLSL's intrinsics, types and texture functions with macros and helpers (`ShaderPrelude`), and spells GLSL reserved words a shader uses as names `we_<word>` for glslang's scanner (`GLSLReservedWords`). glslang preprocesses each stage.
2. On the preprocessed text, by tokens (`GLSLTokenizer`), never by regular expressions on lines: system-value declarations, loop scoping, HLSL's implicit conversions and `mul` (`HLSLConversionPass`), then the pair's linkage (`HLSLLinkage`): varyings located by name in both stages, written inputs and attributes copied into globals, resized and missing varyings, attribute locations, `g_TextureN` bindings and the fragment stage's copies of stage-local uniforms.
3. glslang links both stages under its relaxed Vulkan rules, which gather the loose uniforms into one std140 block `WEUniforms`. In the SPIR-V, the reserved words get WE's names back (`restoreReservedNames`), so the reflection carries WE's names; names MSL can't take (`half`, `this`, a shader's own `log10`) are renamed for the MSL only (`renameMetalClashes`), and SPIRV-Cross spells GLSL keywords its own way there (`_common`).


A wallpaper runs **once**, however many displays show it with the same user properties.

- **The registry.** `WallpaperInstanceRegistry` (`Core/`) holds the running instances, keyed by `WallpaperInstanceKey` (the wallpaper's folder, file and type, and the user-property store it runs with). It belongs to the `WallpaperViewModel` whose displays show them (`sceneInstances`, `videoInstances`), so the Workshop preview window runs its own. Each display holds its instance through a `WallpaperInstanceLease`; the instance stops when no display holds it, one main-queue turn after the last release, so a display that is rebuilt (screens changed) takes hold again first and the wallpaper keeps running. `WallpaperView` keys a display's view by its instance key (`WallpaperViewModel.instanceKeys`), so a display switched to another wallpaper, or to other properties, splits off into that instance.
- **User properties per display.** As in WE, the same wallpaper on two displays has independent user properties (`WallpaperPropertyScope`): each display has its own store (`SceneUserProperties.<identity>.display.<id>`, started from the shared `SceneUserProperties.<identity>`). Settings → Optimizations → "Sync properties across displays" (off by default, WE's "Wallpaper per display") makes every display use the shared store. `WallpaperPropertyGroups` regroups the displays when a wallpaper, the setting or saved properties change: displays of a wallpaper whose stores are equal share one instance (the first display's store), a display whose properties differ runs its own. The sidebar and the inspector edit the selected displays' stores (`WallpaperPropertyTargets`); the running store of an instance is `WallpaperPropertyScope.runtimeKey`. AVKit videos have no properties and keep one player per video.
- **Scenes** (and videos on the Metal path): `SceneWallpaperInstance` owns the loader, one `SceneMetalRenderer` (scripts, particles, timelines, effect graph, sound layers) and the observers. Each display is a `SceneWallpaperPresenter` with its own `MTKView`. With one display the renderer draws straight onto it. With several, the display with the highest frame rate drives (`SceneFrameSchedule`; another takes over if it stops drawing): `renderShared` renders the frame once, at the largest scene target any display needs (`SceneViewport`), through the post-process onto a finished frame; every display then `present(in:)`s it with its own size and placement, one copy pass. The cursor is read from the display it is on, through that display's placement.
- **Loading snapshots.** While a scene loads, each display shows a full-resolution picture of the scene's own frame (`ScenePreviewPlaceholder`), crossfaded to the live scene once it draws: the snapshot for the display's pixel size, else the nearest size scaled, else the Workshop preview. `SceneLoadingSnapshotStore` keeps them as HEIC (JPEG where HEIC can't be written) under `<Caches>/Open Wallpaper Engine/LoadingSnapshots`, keyed by the wallpaper's folder, the display's pixel size and a hash of the folder's top-level files, capped as an LRU. The prepare-on-arrival helper (`--prepare-wallpapers`) writes one per connected display after a second of scene time; a running scene (`SceneLoadingSnapshotCapture`, driven by `SceneRenderLoop`) refreshes its display size once per session, and again after its user properties change, reading the frame back off the render thread. A snapshot is a still (`SceneMetalRenderer.captureStill`): its frame is drawn again without the scene's text layers and clock hands (`SceneClockLayers.stillIDs`: every text object, and the layers whose `angles` script reads the date), as the lock screen and the screen saver show it later and must not show the time it was taken; the displays' frames keep them. Deleting a wallpaper removes its snapshots.
- **AVKit videos:** one `VideoWallpaperViewModel` (one decoding player, one audio player) per video; each display's `AVPlayerView` shows the shared player.
- **Web:** each display keeps its page, except a Chromium page's clone or stretch members, which mirror their source display's page ("Display layouts"). Only the page on the wallpaper's audible display (or mirrored there) plays sound; the others are muted (`WebPageAudio`).
- **Sound** (`WallpaperAudioRouting`): each running wallpaper plays its sound once; a web wallpaper's from its audible display (the main display when it shows it, else the lowest display id), and a wallpaper running as several instances (different properties) from the instance on that display. Different wallpapers on different displays each play theirs. Settings → Optimizations → Audio Output silences all of them; volume and mute (the status menu) apply to all.
- **The watchdog** gets one frame time per rendered frame of an instance, not one per display. Only instances a display can run report: an isolated one (Scene Edit / Export's iPhone & iPad, Android and Screen Saver previews, the Wallpaper Editor's draft, `WallpaperPropertyScope.isIsolated`) never does, so its frames are never blamed on the desktop's wallpapers.

## Display layouts

WE's multi-monitor model (`Library/DisplayLayout/`, the Displays sheet). How to use it: [`display-layouts.md`](display-layouts.md).

- **The layout** (`DisplayLayoutConfiguration`, WE's `wallpaperconfig.layout`, saved in the app's defaults as `DisplayLayout`): a wallpaper per display (0, the default, so per-display wallpapers saved before layouts show as they did), one wallpaper stretched over every display (1, from the main display's selection) or one wallpaper cloned onto every display (2).
- **Groups** (`DisplayGroup`, WE's `profile.groups`), under a wallpaper per display only: a stretch or clone group of some displays beside the others' own wallpapers. Its id is `group_` and an FNV-1a hash of the members, the same on every launch. Displays are named by identity (`DisplayIdentity`: the UUID macOS derives from the display's vendor, model and serial number), not by id. A group with fewer than two connected displays is dormant: kept, and back when its displays are; removing a display from a group of two removes the group.
- **Resolution** (`DisplayLayoutResolution`): the layout on the connected displays, by display id: each clone or stretch member's source display (a clone's main clone display: the chosen one, else the group's first member, under the clone layout the main display; a stretch's first connected member), each stretched display's canvas, each split display's regions, the flipped and the muted displays, and the groups the sheet outlines (a stretch solid, a clone dashed).
- **Clone.** A member shows its main display's wallpaper through the same running instance (`refreshInstanceKeys` gives it the main display's key, and `propertyScope(for:)` its properties), so a scene renders once at the largest target its displays need and each presents it at its own size and placement, an AVKit video has one player (one decode) with a view per display, and a Metal video is one scene. A wallpaper set on a member is set on its main clone display, so the whole clone shows it. A member's own selection stays as it was (WE keeps each monitor's `selectedwallpapers` under a clone): `wallpaper(for:)` resolves what a display shows, and leaving the clone (back to a wallpaper per display, the group removed, or the member taken out) shows the member's own wallpaper again. In Chromium, web pages and WebM videos load once too, on the main clone display (`DisplayLayoutResolution.pageSource`): the other members show a `WebPageMirrorView` (`WebPageMirroring`, `WebPageMirrorRegistry`) fed the browser's IOSurface frames (`ChromiumBrowserPage.addFrameObserver`) into its own Metal layer, covering its display at the scale that fills it. The page pauses only while none of its displays draws, plays the sound when one of them is the audible display, counts as seen while any of their windows is uncovered, and the mouse over a mirror reaches it at the point the mirror shows (`WebPageMirroring.sourcePoint`). On two 1920×1080 displays with a CSS-and-canvas page a clone costs about 40 % less CPU and GPU and 150 MB less memory than a page per display. WebKit keeps a page per display: a `WKWebView` draws in its own window only, snapshots read the page back on the CPU every frame, and Core Animation's private portal layer (`CAPortalLayer`), which draws a layer tree again in another window, measured no better than a second page (the window server's GPU time grew by what the page's fell, and doubled for a WebM clone).
- **Flip** (WE's "Flip clone display"): the window's content is mirrored by a layer transform (`WallpaperWindowContentView`), so the compositor mirrors the frame the display shows and nothing renders again; a scene reads the cursor mirrored there (`NSView.isMirroredOnScreen`). The main clone display can't be flipped, so one member always shows the wallpaper as it is.
- **Mute** (per display, as in WE): a muted display's playback becomes `.mute` (`WallpaperViewModel.displayPlayback`, merged with the playback rules' `rulePlayback`), so a wallpaper's sound (and, for a web page, which display's page plays it) comes from a display that shows it unmuted, and goes quiet when none does (`DisplayPlaybackRouting`). Audio-reactive input is the system's output, as in WE, and stays on.
- **Stretch** (WE's span: the stretch layout and stretch groups). The canvas (`DisplayCanvas`) is the bounding box of the members' desktop rects in global points, as WE's `ui.js` sizes a group: gaps between displays are canvas no display shows, and there's no bezel or density compensation, so each display shows its own rect of the one canvas. Members run the source's instance, as in a clone.
  - *Scene:* the window's content names the canvas (`WallpaperWindowContentView.stretchCanvas`, read into `SceneViewSnapshot.canvas`). A stretched display's `SceneViewport` is the whole canvas at the display's density, so `renderShared` renders one frame for the canvas, at the densest member's pixels (the GPU's largest texture is the only cap, `SceneRenderResolution`), even with one member showing; each display presents its rect (`SceneCanvasSpan`: the frame placed on the canvas, moved by the display's offset, one copy pass). The cursor and parallax read the cursor on the canvas from the display it is on (`SceneViewSnapshot.canvasCursor`), and scripts see the canvas as the screen. A stretched display's picture isn't a loading snapshot.
  - *Video (AVKit):* one player (one decode). Each display's player view is sized to the canvas and offset in its window, which clips it to the display (`View.stretched(on:display:)`): the compositor samples only the display's part. (An `AVPlayerLayer`'s `contentsRect` doesn't reach its video sublayer, so the offset frame does what it would.) A Metal video is a scene.
  - *Web and WebM:* in Chromium the source display's page is sized to the canvas and offset like a video, and the other members mirror it, sized and offset the same way, so each shows its rect of the one canvas-sized page (about 40 % less CPU and GPU and 200 to 380 MB less memory than a page per display). In WebKit each display keeps its own page, sized to the canvas and offset like a video: each page lays out and draws the whole canvas, and only its display's part is composited (one canvas page mirrored through a portal layer cost about 25 % more CPU, as WebKit keeps the tiles outside its window up to date). The pages start together; a page that animates by the clock stays in step, one that keeps its own random state doesn't. On two 1920×1080 Retina displays a stretched page costs about 30 % more CPU and GPU and 50 % more memory than the same page on each display (each page draws twice the area); a stretched scene draws one canvas-sized frame, about 30 % more than one frame for both displays.
- **Splits** (WE's `profile.splits`, under a wallpaper per display, on displays in no group): `{direction, position}` per location, a display's identity or a region's (`<identity>/L`, `/R`, nested), `direction` 0 (WE's "Vertical") side by side and 1 one above the other, `position` the fraction of the width or height from the left or top. `DisplaySplitLayout` divides the display into regions in whole points. Each region is a display of its own, id `<display id>/L…` (`DisplayLayoutResolution.regions`): its own wallpaper, properties and view (`DisplayWallpaperView` lays the regions out in the display's window), its display's playback, mute and enabled state (`routedScreens`). A wallpaper set on a split display goes to its regions; the first region of a new split takes what the display showed, as in WE. WE has no depth limit; its only limit, kept here, is a divider at least a point inside its region (`DisplaySplit.clampedPosition`). A stretch group removes its displays' splits, as WE's does.
- **Copy to / Swap with** (WE's `ui_browse_monitors_copy_to` / `swap_with`, `WallpaperViewModel+DisplayTransfer`): under a wallpaper per display, from a display or region that shows a wallpaper to one outside any group. The wallpaper is set through `setWallpaper`; its properties move between the displays' stores with `WallpaperPropertyTransfer` (WE's `transferWallpaperProperties`: what a store runs, its own or the shared ones, is written to the other, and running stores get the values at once) and its display options with `WallpaperDisplayOptionsStore.copy` / `swap`. A swap of two wallpapers moves each one's settings; one wallpaper on both swaps its two sets. WE also moves per-monitor playlists; playlists here aren't per display.
- **Profiles** (WE's "Save profile" / "Load profile", `DisplayProfiles`): a named copy of the whole layout (layout, groups, splits, flips, mute) and each display's and region's selection, by location, saved as JSON in Application Support (`DisplayProfiles.json`). `DisplayProfiles.load(name:)` is what an app rule's "Load profile" action calls.
- **Screen saver layout** (`ScreenSaverDisplayLayout`, WE's `wallpaperconfigscreensaver = {layout, sameaswallpaper}`, saved as `ScreenSaverDisplayLayout`): "Same as wallpaper" (the default) follows the wallpapers' layout and groups; otherwise each display's own, one stretched or one cloned. See "Lock screen and screen saver".

## Playlists and transitions

How to use them: [`playlists.md`](playlists.md).

- **Timing** (`Library/Playlists/`): `WallpaperPlaylist` stores WE's playlist settings under WE's keys (`mode`, `beginfirst`, `playintro`, `updateonpause`, `transition`, each item's `daytimeend`). `PlaylistSchedule` is the pure maths of the Time of day and Day of week slots; `WallpaperViewModel+PlaylistTiming` runs one timer for the next change (`PlaylistCountdown` for a timer that stands still while paused) and `PlaylistClockObserver` for wake, clock, time zone and day changes. `startPlaylistAtLaunch` applies "When logging in", "Always begin with the first wallpaper" and the slot at launch.
- **Transitions** (`App/Transitions/`): `WallpaperViewModel.setWallpaper(_:for:transition:)` hands a change with a transition to `WallpaperTransitionPerforming` (`WallpaperTransitionCoordinator`), which captures each changing wallpaper's picture (`WallpaperTransitionCapture`: a scene's frame stays on the GPU), applies the change, and plays a `WallpaperTransitionPlayer` per changing wallpaper: `WallpaperTransitionRenderer` (the Metal port of WE's transition shader) draws each frame off the main thread (`WallpaperTransitionFrameLoop`: a `CAMetalDisplayLink` on a thread of its own, on WE's clock, `WallpaperTransitionClock`) into the Metal layer of each display's overlay (`WallpaperTransitionOverlayView`, in the display options' transform view) over the live incoming wallpaper, placed by `WallpaperTransitionGeometry` (one render for a clone or stretch, copied to the other displays' drawables). At the Verbose log level each transition logs its frame intervals and main-thread stalls (`WallpaperTransitionMetrics`). A later change applies one still capturing first.

## Isolated edits (Scene Edit / Export's Screen Saver and export modes)

- **The session.** A mode that previews and renders its own version of a wallpaper (the Screen Saver and iPhone & iPad Export modes) opens an `IsolatedSceneEditSession` (`Scene/UI/`). It copies the edited store's values (user properties and Scene Edit / Export's layer edits) into an isolated store, `WallpaperPropertyScope.isolated(<purpose>)`, saved under that suffix and run under its own runtime key. Scene Edit / Export's own models are pointed at that scope, so the mode's layer and property edits use the same code as the Wallpaper mode; `setValues` and `setLayerVisible` do the same from code. A save to an isolated store doesn't regroup the displays.
- **The private instance.** `IsolatedSceneView` runs the wallpaper from the session's own `WallpaperInstanceRegistry` under `WallpaperInstanceKey(wallpaper, properties: .isolated(…))`: never the displays' shared instance, silent (a preview screen), and without loading snapshots, so the desktop's snapshots and lock-screen picture don't change.
- **The render hook.** `values` is everything an offscreen render of that version takes: the Live Photo job's properties (`LivePhotoJob`), rendered by the helper with exactly these. `replaceValues` swaps the whole store for a mode's own saved version (the Screen Saver mode's choices).
- **Lifetime.** Leaving the mode, closing the Scene Edit / Export window or showing another wallpaper ends the session: the isolated store is removed and its running store emptied.
- **Which modes show** (`SceneEditorModes`): every mode for a scene; for a video, Screen Saver, iPhone & iPad Export and Android Export with no Wallpaper mode (a file AVFoundation can't read shows the first two with why); for a web wallpaper, Wallpaper and an unavailable Android Export with WE's message. An unavailable mode shows its reason in place of its editor. All exporting happens in these modes; the library has none.

## Live Photo export (`LivePhoto/`)

How to use it: [`iphone-ipad-export.md`](iphone-ipad-export.md).

- The iPhone & iPad Export mode frames the private instance as the chosen device's lock screen (`DeviceModel`, `LockScreenLayout`, `LivePhotoCrop`); its right-hand panel is the selected layer's adjustments and the export's progress (`LivePhotoExportLayerPanel`), and the Export Settings (`LivePhotoExportSettingsView`) are the toolbar's sheet, with the exports and Export More.
- The helper run `--render-live-photo <job.json>` (`LivePhotoRenderer`) renders offscreen through the real loader and renderer. A motion job renders the first 8 s small and writes each frame's difference from the last (`LivePhotoMotion`, `ScreenSaverFrameSignature`); the app moves the clip to the window with the most motion. An export renders the clip into a near-lossless intermediate movie while choosing the still (`LivePhotoKeyFrame`), writes the HEIC, then encodes the movie (`LivePhotoMovieEncoder`, `IntermediateReader`; at most 1920 px on its long side, `moviePixels`) with the lock screen's metadata (`LivePhotoMetadata`: a `live-photo-info` sample per frame, and still-image-time with the still's transform at the still's frame, never before 0.5 s, `LivePhotoKeyFrame.earliestSeconds`) and a crossfade into the still at both ends (`ScreenSaverSeamFinder.crossfadeWeight`).
- A video wallpaper's Live Photo goes through the same helper run and writer: `LivePhotoRenderer.render` reads the video's frames (`LivePhotoVideoFrames`: `AVAssetReader` in order, the latest frame at or before each time of the clip's grid, looping at the video's end, turned by the track's transform and cut to the crop in Core Image) in place of the scene renderer. The crop is measured in the video's picture as it plays (`SceneEditorModes.videoSize`), and the preview plays the file (`LoopingVideoFileView`).
- With "Also Save to Photos Album" on, the pair goes into a regular Photos album through PhotoKit (`LivePhotoAlbumSync` over `LivePhotoLibrary`, `PhotoKitLibrary`).
- **Batches** ("Export More with These Settings…", `LivePhotoExportModel+Batch`, `LivePhotoBatchQueue`, `LivePhotoBatchExporter`, `LivePhotoBatchExportSheet`): the picked wallpapers become items with the mode's device, quality and clip (`LivePhotoBatchTemplate`; each framed for its own size, centred, its own motion window when the mode's is automatic) and the edited one with its own settings and values; scenes render one at a time, videos beside them (`ExportLanes`). Each finished pair is copied into the chosen folder and saved to the Photos album when those are on, and stays in the export cache until the sheet closes, for "AirDrop All" (`airDropItems`: each Live Photo as its `LivePhotoBundle`, a `.pvt` package with Photos' `metadata.plist`, which iOS imports as one Live Photo; the loose pair arrives as a photo and a video) and each item's own AirDrop.

## Android export (`AndroidExport/`)

WE's "Export .mpkg" for its Android app (Scene Edit / Export's Android Export mode, one wallpaper or a batch; `export_android` for MCP clients). All exporting happens in Scene Edit / Export; the library has no export command. Ground truth is WE 2.8.42's exports (`we-test-wp-images`, `android-transfer/MPKG.md`), which the WE app on a tablet imports and plays.
